title: Jadabharatha Charitram
body:
Jadabharatha Charitram

Long before he was known as Jadabharatha, he was King Bharatha, a ruler so noble that this vast land, Bharata, is said to have been named after him. His reign was prosperous and his people content, yet he understood that all worldly glory is fleeting, and in time he renounced his throne and retreated into the forest to devote himself to the worship of Sriman Narayana on the banks of the river Gandaki. There, in deep meditation, the power of his penance grew until he stood upon the very threshold of moksha.
But fate is never without its trials. One day, as he sat in contemplation by the river, he saw a pregnant deer leap across the water in terror as a tiger gave chase. In its desperate bound the doe's sack broke, and the newborn fawn fell into the flowing current, landing upon a floating leaf. Bharatha broke his worship, lifted the trembling creature from the water, and carried it to his hermitage. What began as simple compassion slowly became attachment. He dedicated all his time to the fawn, and his meditation grew distracted; when he sat for penance his mind would wander to the deer — was it safe, had it strayed too far? The fawn grew into a deer and eventually returned to the forest, but the bond had already taken root in his heart.
And so, when Bharatha's own time came to depart his body, his final thoughts were not of the Lord but of the deer. It is said that whatever fills the mind in its dying moment shapes the next birth, and Bharatha, who had once been on the cusp of liberation, was reborn as a deer. Yet even in that form some memory remained, and he lingered near the hermitages of sages, drawn to the chanting of the Lord's name. When that life ended he was born once more, this time into a scholarly brahmana family, with the wisdom of his past lives intact.
But he had learned the danger of attachment, and he resolved never again to be entangled in the affairs of the world. So he remained silent. He never reacted, never spoke unnecessarily, never sought praise or feared insult. Because of this his own family took him for a fool, incapable of learning, and set him to the most menial labor, which he performed with perfect detachment. From this apparent dullness he earned the name Jada — the dull one — and became a nomad wandering the forests. Once a band of cannibals seized him to sacrifice to Goddess Kali, but the Goddess herself, recognizing that he had attained the state of renunciation, rejected the offering and spared him.
One day, as Jadabharatha roamed the forest, the royal palanquin of King Rahuguna came passing by. A bearer had grown weak, and, seeing this well-built man, the carriers forced him into service. But Jadabharatha would not walk as the others did; he stepped slowly and carefully, avoiding even the ants upon the path, so that the palanquin jolted unevenly. Irritated, the king rebuked him — he seemed strong, yet he was so slow and lazy. Jadabharatha answered that he was neither strong nor weak, neither active nor lazy, neither fast nor slow. Taking him for a madman, the king demanded an explanation, and at last Jadabharatha spoke.
He told the king that when he described himself, he had not been speaking of his body but of his soul. The soul, he said, has no form and performs no action; it is imperishable, untouched by the burdens the body bears. If one asks another for water, it is brought in a vessel, though only the water was sought — and just so, the body is only a vessel for the soul, as the soul in turn is a vessel for the paramatma. He who commands the bearer commands only the body, not the self within it. These were not the words of a fool but of one who had seen beyond the illusion of the world. Shaken, Rahuguna descended from his palanquin and fell at Jadabharatha's feet, and Jadabharatha taught him the nature of the self, the impermanence of the body, and the truth that liberation comes not from conquest but from surrender. The king departed transformed, and Jadabharatha, his final duty fulfilled, disappeared once more into the forest, leaving behind only the echo of his wisdom.
